strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: conventional TTA evaluation ignores the latency cost of adaptation, which matters for real deployment (edge devices, interactive systems, budget-constrained missions).

The three proposed metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) are well-motivated by distinct, realistic deployment archetypes and are each accompanied by a clear formal protocol and interpretable decomposition (availability/served-accuracy, responsiveness/accuracy, adapted/frozen accuracy).

Careful, explicit engagement with prior work (Alfarra et al., 2024): the paper identifies concrete limitations (risk-free fallback, disproportionate ceiling penalties, forced idling) and proposes a principled buffered single-model alternative, with a full appendix justifying design choices.

Extensive empirical study: 7 TTA methods × 15 corruptions × 16 temporal scenarios (240 evaluations), with detailed per-corruption and per-scenario decompositions in the appendix that substantiate the main claims (e.g., Tables 3–5, 13–19).

The findings are actionable and non-trivial in their specificity: e.g., quantifying exactly how much accuracy improvement would be needed to overcome availability/responsiveness penalties (computational insolvency), and identifying SHOT-IM's surprising resilience under budget exhaustion due to full-backbone updates.

Good transparency about scope and limitations in the Discussion section (single dataset/architecture, exclusions of certain method classes, episodic i.i.d. assumption), and honest treatment of when methods are mismatched to evaluation context (e.g., LAME).
weaknesses: All experiments use a single architecture (ResNet-50), single dataset/benchmark (ImageNet-C), and single hardware platform (RTX 4080 GPU); despite claims that findings generalize, no evidence is given across different backbones, tasks, or especially embedded/edge hardware, which is central to several of the paper's own motivating examples (drones, wildlife cameras, on-device photo apps).

Results are reported from a single seed with no variance or statistical significance testing (explicitly acknowledged), which weakens confidence in close rank comparisons and the reported Spearman correlations.

The contribution is purely evaluative/diagnostic; no new adaptation method or mitigation strategy is proposed to address the identified failure modes (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, unproductive overhead), somewhat limiting the paper's forward-looking impact beyond providing a benchmark lens.

The set of evaluated methods, while reasonable, is relatively dated (Tent 2021, ETA/SAR 2022–2023); the exclusion of more recent multi-forward-pass or wrapper-based methods (justified in the Discussion) limits the currency of the specific empirical conclusions, even though the framework itself would still apply.

Some design choices (hyperbolic decay for continuous utility, specific ρ/T/B grids) are reasonable but not deeply validated against real user studies or system telemetry; the practical translation of these thresholds to arbitrary deployments is left largely to informal analogy (e.g., drone battery, photo app) rather than grounded empirical calibration.

The core high-level finding that gradient-based methods with heavier backward-pass overhead lose out under tight temporal budgets is somewhat expected a priori from known accuracy-cost trade-offs in the TTA literature; the paper's novelty rests more on quantifying and systematizing this than on revealing a wholly unexpected phenomenon.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: conventional TTA evaluation ignores the accuracy-latency trade-off that governs real deployability, and the paper makes a compelling case (with concrete deployment vignettes) for why this matters.

The three utility metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) are each grounded in distinct, well-motivated deployment archetypes (hard-deadline streams, interactive/HCI settings, budget-constrained edge devices) rather than being an arbitrary single metric.

Careful, critical engagement with prior work (Alfarra et al., 2024): the paper identifies three concrete limitations (risk-free fallback evaluation, disproportionate ceiling penalties, forced idling) and proposes a buffered single-model protocol that addresses them, with clear justification in Appendix B.

Extensive empirical scope: 7 methods x 15 corruptions x multiple parameter settings = 240 evaluations, with thorough decomposition tables (availability, responsiveness, adapted/frozen accuracy) that explain *why* rankings invert rather than just reporting that they do.

The utility decompositions surface actionable, non-obvious findings (e.g., SHOT-IM's superior frozen-state stability, the disproportionate cost of backpropagation as 'extrinsic overhead', computational insolvency thresholds) that could genuinely inform future TTA method design.
Clear writing, well-organized figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 3), and thorough appendices with notation tables, method descriptions, and per-corruption breakdowns that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Results are reported for a single random seed (explicitly noted in Appendix C.2/C.3) with no variance estimates or significance testing, despite the paper making fine-grained quantitative claims (e.g., Spearman rs = -0.74 vs 0.21, 41.2% loss rate, 19.3% average utility gap) that would benefit from uncertainty quantification, especially given the central thesis is about rank *instability*.

Evaluation is confined to a single architecture (ResNet-50), single dataset (ImageNet-C), and single hardware platform (RTX 4080); latency-based conclusions (e.g., magnitude of extrinsic overhead, specific insolvency thresholds) are inherently hardware- and implementation-dependent, and the paper's claim in the Discussion that the 'underlying need... remains universal' across modalities/architectures/hardware is asserted rather than empirically supported.

The specific functional forms chosen for the metrics (hyperbolic decay with HCI-motivated threshold T, single-batch buffer size, geometric spacing of parameter sweeps) are reasonable but somewhat heuristic design choices rather than derived from a principled model of user/system utility; sensitivity of conclusions to these choices is not examined.

The evaluation remains restricted to the episodic, i.i.d. corruption-shift setting, which the paper itself notes is a mismatch for methods like LAME designed for non-i.i.d. streams (which then trivially underperforms in all 240 cases); this raises the question of how much the reported 'rank instability' is confounded by evaluation-method mismatch versus genuine temporal-pressure effects.

The core methodological contribution builds incrementally on Alfarra et al. (2024)'s discrete formulation, extending it with two additional metrics and a protocol refinement; while valuable, the conceptual novelty is more in scope/systematization than in fundamentally new technique.
No code/artifact availability statement is visible in the excerpted text beyond a mention of a 'supplementary code repository', making full reproducibility hard to verify from the manuscript alone.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in TTA evaluation: the accuracy-latency trade-off is typically ignored in offline benchmarking despite being critical for real deployments.

The three utility metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) are well-motivated, grounded in physical units (ms) rather than model-relative proxies, and each is accompanied by a clear decomposition (availability, responsiveness, adapt/frozen accuracy) that provides interpretable diagnosis of failure modes rather than just aggregate numbers.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 750+ temporal evaluations across 11 TTA methods, multiple architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ResNet-18), multiple datasets (ImageNet-C, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-V2, CIFAR-10-C), and multiple hardware platforms (RTX 4080 GPU, Raspberry Pi 5 CPU), demonstrating that the central finding (rank instability) generalizes broadly.

Careful, well-justified revision of prior work's (Alfarra et al.) discrete evaluation protocol, addressing concrete flaws (risk-free fallback, disproportionate penalties, forced idling) with a principled buffered single-model design, and transparent side-by-side comparison in the appendix.

The failure-mode analysis (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, harmful adaptation) leads to concrete, well-argued design principles (corruption-conditioned compute allocation, time-aware scaling, anytime performance) that give actionable guidance for future TTA method design.

Strong attention to reproducibility and transparency: detailed appendices document implementation choices (e.g., batch-norm running-buffer handling), timing methodology, and provide per-batch decomposition tables; code is promised for release.
Honest and specific limitations discussion (single seed, exclusion of certain method classes, episodic i.i.d. assumption) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: All main experiments are run with a single seed; while the authors claim seed variance is negligible (citing prior work), no direct variance/error bars are reported for Tempora's own metrics, which is a concern given some utility gaps between methods are small (e.g., a few percentage points in Table 23).

The evaluation remains restricted to episodic, i.i.d. batch sampling, which is acknowledged as a mismatch for continual/non-stationary methods (e.g., LAME's uniform failure), potentially limiting how far conclusions transfer to more realistic streaming conditions; this is left entirely to future work rather than even a preliminary exploration.

Design choices within each utility metric (hyperbolic discounting form for continuous utility, single-batch buffer size for discrete, fixed batch size of 64) are motivated qualitatively but not stress-tested with sensitivity analyses, so it is unclear how robust the reported rank instability is to these modeling choices.

The headline qualitative finding—that offline rankings do not predict rankings under latency pressure, and that slower/more sophisticated gradient-based methods lose out—is intuitive given the construction of the metrics (overhead directly penalizes availability/responsiveness); the paper's main novelty lies more in the systematic measurement framework than in a surprising empirical discovery, which somewhat limits the significance of the core result relative to the depth of engineering effort.

Method coverage, while reasonable, excludes several relevant TTA variants (DDA, MEMO, wrapper-style methods) that the authors themselves note could interact interestingly with temporal constraints, and this exclusion is justified more by tractability than principled scoping.

Hardware diversity for the main results is limited to one GPU; the CPU-based experiments use only a single low-power edge device (Raspberry Pi) with a different backbone/dataset (ResNet-18/CIFAR-10-C) rather than being integrated into the main ImageNet-C/ResNet-50 or ViT-B/16 analysis, making cross-hardware comparisons somewhat fragmented across separate mini-studies.
